title: Circuits with a closed-form solution: dividers, an RC filter and series RLC circuits

cases.title: Voltage divider of 1 kohm and 3 kohm on 10 V
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: a linear solve of a three-node circuit, so only rounding is accepted
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the voltage-divider circuit: Vout = Vin R2/(R1 + R2)

cases.title: Loaded divider: 1 kohm over two 1 kohm resistors in parallel on 10 V
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the parallel pair is 500 ohm, so Vout = 10 x 500/1500 exactly up to rounding
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, resistors in parallel and the voltage-divider circuit

cases.title: First-order RC low-pass: gain at the corner frequency
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: C = 1/(2 pi R f) for f = 1 kHz, so |H| = 1/sqrt(2) up to the rounding of C
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, frequency response of the first-order low-pass filter: |H(j w_c)| = 1/sqrt(2) at w_c = 1/(R C)

cases.title: First-order RC low-pass: phase at the corner frequency
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the phase is -arctan(w R C) = -45 degrees up to the rounding of C
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, frequency response of the first-order low-pass filter: phase = -arctan(w/w_c)

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF): gain across the resistor at resonance
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: at f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)) the reactances cancel, so the resistor takes the whole source voltage
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the series RLC band-pass: at the resonant frequency w0 = 1/sqrt(LC) the output across R equals the input

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF): gain across the capacitor at resonance equals Q
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: at resonance the capacitor voltage is Q = sqrt(L/C)/R times the source, exactly up to rounding of the frequency
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the series RLC circuit: at w0 the voltage across the capacitor is Q times the source with Q = (1/R) sqrt(L/C)

cases.title: RC step response after one time constant
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: wider than the error of the trapezoidal rule at 100 steps per time constant plus the first backward Euler step and the 1 ns rise of the source
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the step response of an RC circuit: v(t) = V (1 - exp(-t/(R C))), which is 1 - 1/e = 0.6321 at t = R C

cases.title: Underdamped series RLC step response at 100 us
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: wider than the error of the trapezoidal rule at 1000 steps over three quarters of a ring period, the first backward Euler step and the 1 ns rise of the source
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, the step response of a series RLC circuit, underdamped: v(t) = V (1 - exp(-a t) (cos(wd t) + (a/wd) sin(wd t))) with a = R/(2L) = 5000 1/s and wd = sqrt(1/(L C) - a^2) = 31224.99 rad/s

cases.title: Diode with a 1 kohm series resistor on 5 V (IS 1e-14 A, n 1): voltage across the diode
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: Newton-Raphson stops when the change is below reltol*|v| + vntol twice in a row, which leaves an error of about 1e-5 V on the junction voltage, so 1e-4 V is wider than needed and still far below the 26 mV scale of the junction
cases.source: Shockley ideal diode equation I = Is (exp(Vd/(n Vt)) - 1) with Vt = k T / q (k = 1.380649e-23 J/K, q = 1.602176634e-19 C, T = 300.15 K, the temperature of config/sim.cfg), A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the diode forward characteristic; the series circuit Vs = I R + Vd has the closed form I = (n Vt / R) W((Is R / (n Vt)) exp((Vs + Is R) / (n Vt))) - Is with W the principal branch of the Lambert W function (R. M. Corless, G. H. Gonnet, D. E. G. Hare, D. J. Jeffrey and D. E. Knuth, On the Lambert W function, Advances in Computational Mathematics 5, 1996); W was evaluated by Newton iteration on ln w + w = ln x and checked against a bisection of the same equation

cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the reverse current is IS plus the conductance gmin (1e-12 S) times 5 V, about 5e-12 A, which is 1.1e-8 V across 2.2 kohm
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the half-wave rectifier: the diode does not conduct while the source is negative, so the load carries no current

cases.title: Inverting amplifier with 1 kohm and 2 kohm and an op-amp of gain 1e6, input 1 V: output
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the ideal gain is -R2/R1; the finite open-loop gain 1e6 of the model lowers it by the factor 1 + (1 + R2/R1)/A = 1 + 3e-6, which is 6e-6 V at 2 V, so 2e-5 V is wider than that error
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the inverting configuration of an ideal op-amp: Vout/Vin = -R2/R1

cases.title: Voltage-controlled switch (on 100 ohm) closed by a 5 V control into a 900 ohm load on 5 V: load voltage
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the control is 2.5 V above the threshold with a transition half width of 0.1 V, so the conductance is within 1e-21 of its on value and the divider is exact up to rounding
cases.source: voltage divider of the on resistance and the load (J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits): Vout = 5 x 900/(900 + 100)

cases.title: Voltage-controlled switch (off 1e9 ohm) opened by a 0 V control into a 900 ohm load on 5 V: load voltage
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the control is 2.5 V below the threshold, so the conductance is within 1e-21 of its off value and the divider is exact up to rounding
cases.source: voltage divider of the off resistance and the load (J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits): Vout = 5 x 900/(900 + 1e9)

cases.title: RC step response: 10 % to 90 % rise time of a 1 kohm and 1 uF circuit
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the trapezoidal rule with a step of 10 us (a hundredth of the time constant) and a straight line between the points leave an error below 1e-4, and the swing is taken up to 10 time constants
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the response of an STC network to a step: the 10 % to 90 % rise time is ln(9) tau = 2.2 tau with tau = R C

cases.title: RC step response with R1 stepped over 1, 2 and 4 kohm: rise time of the third run
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the rise time is proportional to R, so the third run (4 kohm, tau = 4 ms) takes ln(9) x 4 ms; the step of 20 us is a two-hundredth of tau
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, the response of an STC network to a step: tr = ln(9) tau with tau = R C

cases.title: First-order RC low-pass: -3 dB frequency from the AC sweep
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the level is taken 3.01 dB below the gain at the first frequency of the sweep (10 Hz, 1e-4 below the gain at zero frequency) and the crossing is interpolated in the logarithm of the frequency with 100 points per decade, which leaves about 1e-4
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, frequency response of the first-order low-pass filter: the cutoff frequency is f_c = 1/(2 pi R C)

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF) across the resistor: -3 dB bandwidth
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the two -3 dB frequencies are interpolated in the logarithm of the frequency with 100 points per decade, which leaves about 2e-5 on the width
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, series RLC band-pass filter: the half-power bandwidth is beta = R/L rad/s, that is R/(2 pi L) in hertz

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF) across the resistor: quality factor of the band-pass response
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the peak frequency is refined by a parabola through three points and the width by interpolation, 100 points per decade, which leaves about 2e-5
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, series RLC band-pass filter: Q = f0/B = (1/R) sqrt(L/C)

cases.title: Second-order low-pass with Q = 1/sqrt(2) (44.72 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF): quality factor from the phase
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the gain at the frequency where the phase is -90 degrees over the gain at the first frequency (10 Hz), both interpolated in the logarithm of the frequency with 100 points per decade, which leaves about 1e-4
cases.source: A. S. Sedra and K. C. Smith, Microelectronic Circuits, second-order low-pass filters: the phase is -90 degrees at w0 where the gain is Q times the gain at DC, and Q = 1/sqrt(2) is the maximally flat (Butterworth) response; for the series RLC circuit across the capacitor Q = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) (J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits)

cases.title: Loop of two poles with the closed loop of a Butterworth response (zeta = 1/sqrt(2)): phase margin
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the integrator is a transconductance into 1 uF with a leak of 1 Gohm, a pole at 1.6e-4 Hz that moves the margin by less than 1e-4 degrees; the interpolation at 100 points per decade leaves 3e-4 degrees
cases.source: K. Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, second-order system: for L(s) = wn^2/(s(s + 2 zeta wn)) the phase margin is atan(2 zeta/sqrt(sqrt(1 + 4 zeta^4) - 2 zeta^2)), 65.53 degrees for zeta = 1/sqrt(2)

cases.title: Loop K/(1 + s/w0)^3 with K = 4: gain margin
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the phase and the gain are interpolated in the logarithm of the frequency with 100 points per decade, which leaves 7e-4 dB
cases.source: K. Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, stability margins: L(s) = K/(1 + s/w0)^3 has phase -180 degrees at w = sqrt(3) w0 where |L| = K/8, so the gain margin is 20 log10(8/K) = 6.02 dB for K = 4

cases.title: Loop K/(1 + s/w0)^3 with K = 4: phase margin
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the unity-gain frequency and the phase are interpolated in the logarithm of the frequency with 100 points per decade, which leaves 2e-3 degrees
cases.source: K. Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, stability margins: |L| = 1 where (1 + x^2)^(3/2) = K, so the phase margin is 180 - 3 atan(sqrt(K^(2/3) - 1)) degrees (27.14 degrees for K = 4)

cases.title: Thermal noise of a 1 kohm resistor at 27 degrees Celsius: voltage density
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the density is flat, sqrt(4 k T R) with k = 1.380649e-23 J/K (exact in the SI since 2019, CODATA 2018) and T = 300.15 K, the 27 degrees Celsius of config/sim.cfg, so only rounding is accepted
cases.source: J. B. Johnson, Phys. Rev. 32, 97 (1928) and H. Nyquist, Phys. Rev. 32, 110 (1928): the open-circuit noise voltage of a resistor is e_n^2 = 4 k T R per hertz; the Boltzmann constant is the one of the SI brochure (BIPM, 9th edition)

cases.title: Thermal noise of a 1 kohm resistor across 1 uF: total noise voltage
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the density 4 k T R/(1 + (2 pi f R C)^2) is integrated by the trapezoidal rule over twelve decades with 100 points per decade, which leaves 4e-5; the bands below 1 mHz and above 1 GHz hold less than 1e-6 of the power
cases.source: H. Nyquist, Phys. Rev. 32, 110 (1928): integrating 4 k T R over the power gain 1/(1 + (2 pi f R C)^2) with the integral of df/(1 + (2 pi f R C)^2) = 1/(4 R C) gives a mean square of k T/C, whatever R is

cases.title: Divider of two 1 kohm resistors with uniform tolerances of 1 %: deviation of the output over 4000 runs
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the sample deviation of 4000 draws has a relative standard error near 1 %, and 6 % is six of them; the second-order terms of the propagation are below 1e-3
cases.source: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data - Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement, 5.1.2 equation (10): u(V)^2 = sum (dV/dRi)^2 u(Ri)^2, with dV/dR1 = -2.5e-3 V/ohm, dV/dR2 = +2.5e-3 V/ohm and, for a rectangular distribution of half width a, u = a/sqrt(3) (4.3.7), here 10/sqrt(3) ohm; the result is sqrt(2) x 2.5e-3 x 10/sqrt(3)

cases.title: Divider of two 1 kohm resistors with uniform tolerances of 1 %: mean of the output over 4000 runs
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the mean of 4000 draws has a standard error of 3.2e-4 V, and 3 mV is nine of them; the bias of the second order is 4e-5 V
cases.source: JCGM 100:2008, Evaluation of measurement data - Guide to the expression of uncertainty in measurement, 5.1.2: to first order the expected value of the output is its value at the expected values of the inputs, 10 x 1000/2000 = 5 V

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF) step response: peak value
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: zeta = (R/2) sqrt(C/L) = 0.158; the trapezoidal rule with a step of 1 us (a thirtieth of the period of oscillation) and the first step of backward Euler leave about 5e-4 on the peak
cases.source: K. Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, second-order system: the peak overshoot of the step response is Mp = exp(-pi zeta/sqrt(1 - zeta^2)), so the peak of a unit step is 1 + Mp

cases.title: First-order RC low-pass (1 kohm, 1 uF): pole frequency from the rational fit
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the response is exactly rational of order one, so the fit is exact up to rounding
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, first-order circuits: the natural response decays with s = -1/(R C)

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF) across the capacitor: frequency of the poles from the rational fit
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the response is exactly rational of order two, so the fit is exact up to rounding and the conditioning of the fit
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, natural response of the series RLC circuit: s = -alpha +- sqrt(alpha^2 - w0^2) with alpha = R/(2L) and w0 = 1/sqrt(L C), so the poles are at |s| = w0

cases.title: Series RLC (10 ohm, 1 mH, 1 uF) across the capacitor: quality factor of the poles from the rational fit
cases.tolerance_note: chosen here: the response is exactly rational of order two, so the fit is exact up to rounding and the conditioning of the fit
cases.source: J. W. Nilsson and S. A. Riedel, Electric Circuits, natural response of the series RLC circuit: Q = w0/(2 alpha) = (1/R) sqrt(L/C)
